children.text: An armoured shell, not a reinforced booth

The Bulletproof Security Cabin is a guard post built around an armoured outer shell rather than a standard cabin body with plating added to it. The exterior is clad in armour steel panels, the glazed areas use bullet-resistant laminated glass, and the doors are steel-framed with high-security locking. That combination is what separates it from an ordinary observation booth: the structure is intended to protect the person inside, not simply to give them somewhere to stand and watch the approach.
Protection is specified for the project

The armour panels and glazing are produced to international ballistic resistance standards and have been through ballistic testing. What the standard does not do is fix a single level across the range — cabins are built to different ballistic classes, and the class is agreed for the project rather than being a fixed property of the model. Where a scheme has to meet a particular resistance level, that level needs to be set out at the point of order.
Room to work, and room for equipment

The range runs from 1.50m × 1.50m up to 3.00m × 5.00m. The smallest sizes are single-occupant posts, sized so that one officer has a working position and a clear view out without carrying more structure than the location can take. The mid sizes add space for monitors, radio equipment, camera control panels and document storage alongside the operator. At the wide end, two or more personnel can work at once and the cabin functions as a small control point or temporary coordination centre rather than only a checkpoint — with room for computers, communications equipment, secure storage and, on the largest models, an area to stand down between shifts.
Fitted out for long shifts

Interiors are lined to provide heat and sound insulation, and lighting, ventilation, air conditioning, power outlets and the cabling for communications and security panels can be built in before the cabin leaves the works. Cabins arrive ready for use, so bringing one into service is a matter of siting it rather than fitting it out on the ground.
Heavy, but still movable

For all the weight of the shell, these are modular structures rather than fixed buildings. A cabin is placed with a forklift or crane and can be lifted again and moved to another position when the picture on the ground changes, which is what makes it usable for temporary postings as well as permanent ones.

children.text: A moulded polyester shell, built to stand outside

The GRP Cabin is a modular cabin moulded from glass reinforced polyester, and the material is what the range is built around. Polyester holds up against sun, rain and wind, which is what gives the cabin its working life outdoors, and its insulating properties keep the interior comfortable in both summer and winter.

The shell is light for its size. That makes a cabin straightforward to transport and to relocate if the site plan changes later — useful on construction sites and event grounds, where a control point rarely stays in one place for the life of the project.
Delivered ready for use
Cabins arrive complete, so putting one into service is a matter of siting the unit rather than building it. The same holds if it needs to move again.
Five sizes, from a single pitch to a shared control room

The range runs from 1.50m × 1.50m up to 2.70m × 2.70m. The smaller sizes suit a confined pitch where one person needs shelter and a clear view of the approach. The wider models give enough floor area for more than one member of staff, and enough room to bring in additional equipment or furniture where the role calls for it.
Where GRP Cabins are used
Security and control points
at site, factory and residential entrances.
Car parks and valet services
, where staff need shelter without losing sight of the approach.
Construction sites
, as a temporary management office or observation booth.
Events and organisations
, as a ticket control or management cabin.
Sales and service kiosks
— food and drink counters, bread distribution points, and newspaper or small retail stands.

children.text: Sandwich panel walls, insulated against heat and noise

The Insulated Panel Cabin is built from sandwich panel, and that construction is what the range is organised around. The panel walls hold back heat and sound together, so the person on duty is kept off the worst of the summer and out of the winter cold, and works in a space that is isolated from the noise going on outside it. Wind, rain and direct sun are kept out the same way, which is what lets the cabin stand outdoors for years rather than for a season.

The outside asks very little in return. The cladding wipes clean and needs no routine attention to stay presentable, so a cabin that has been on the gate for a long time still looks like part of the organisation rather than something left over from the last project.
Delivered wired, ready to be sited

Cabins arrive with the electrics already in place — lighting and socket outlets fitted inside, and the connections prepared for mains power and water. Ventilation comes as part of the build. Nothing has to be constructed on site: no foundations, no fitting-out, no second trade after the delivery lorry has gone, which is what makes the range worth considering for short-term work as well as for a permanent post.
Moving one later is equally undemanding. A forklift or a crane lifts the cabin and sets it down wherever it is wanted, and it can be lifted again and reused somewhere else when the site plan changes.
Five sizes, from a single post to a shared office

The range runs from 1.10m × 1.10m up to 2.60m × 2.60m. The smallest models are made for a confined pitch where one person needs shelter and a clear line of sight to the approach, and they take up little enough ground to drop into a gateway or a kerbside that has no room to spare.

The middle of the range gives a single member of staff a proper working position — enough floor for a desk and chair, and for a control panel or the equipment the role happens to need. The largest sizes go further again, holding desks, seating, a cabinet and control screens, and taking several people on duty at once. Generous glazing brings daylight into the larger models, which matters on a long shift.
Where insulated panel cabins are used
Security and control points
at estate gates, factory and warehouse entrances, and school and hospital campuses.
Car parks and valet services
, where staff need somewhere sheltered to work and store the equipment that goes with the job.
Reception and visitor control
, greeting arrivals and directing them at a private entrance or a building forecourt.
Construction sites and logistics centres
, as a site enquiries point or a temporary office.
Events and public venues
— exhibitions, concerts, sporting fixtures and municipal service points, where a ticket or control cabin is needed for a fixed run of dates and then moved on.

children.text: An aluminium composite skin over an insulated shell

The KompoCity Composite Cabin is built in two layers: a sandwich panel structure inside, clad on the outside in aluminium composite panel. That cladding is what separates the range from an ordinary site cabin. It stands up to rain, sun and wind, and it avoids the fading and rusting that show up on an exterior surface after a few seasons outdoors.

The inner sandwich panel does the other half of the work. It insulates against heat and sound, so staff on a long shift are not sitting in whatever the weather is doing outside, and the interior lining is chosen to keep even the smaller cabins feeling open rather than boxed in.
A frontage that suits the building behind it

A cabin at the entrance to a development, a hotel or a business centre becomes part of the frontage whether or not anyone intended it to. The composite exterior gives straight lines and a smooth, even surface, which sits closer to the architecture around it than a traditional security booth does. Colour and cladding details can be matched to an organisation's identity, and logos can be applied to the panels.
Modular, so it can move

Cabins are modular and go up quickly once on site. A unit can be lifted with a forklift or crane, taken to another part of the site or to another site entirely, and put back into service there — useful where a control point moves with the phase of a project rather than staying at one gate for good.

Interiors can be prepared before delivery: electrical installation, lighting, sockets and ventilation, with air conditioning infrastructure where the role calls for it. The cabin arrives set up for the job it is going to do.
Five sizes, from a single pitch to a working office

The range runs from 1.40m × 1.40m up to 2.65m × 2.65m. The smallest is sized for one person on duty, and its compact footprint is an advantage in a city centre, a plaza or a shopping centre entrance where there is little floor area to give up. The middle of the range takes a desk, a chair and a document rack. The larger cabins hold a desk, seating, filing, monitors and communications equipment with room to receive a visitor, and there is space for a small sink or an air conditioning unit where the cabin is doing more than watching a gate.
Where composite cabins are used
Security and gatehouse duty
at residential developments, hotels, campuses and school entrances.
Information and reception points
in front of public buildings, university campuses and cultural centres.
Valet and car park reception
, at car park and restaurant entrances.
Sales offices
at outdoor events, fairs and temporary stands.
Kiosks and ticket points
— cafeteria counters, ticket and travel card sales, and small service points in areas with heavy foot traffic.

children.text: Betopan outside, sandwich panel inside

The MetroCity Modular Cabin is built from two materials working to different ends. The exterior is clad in Betopan, and that cladding is what the cabin shows to the street. It holds its appearance outdoors — sunlight, rain, humidity and wind leave it without fading, cracking or peeling — and it takes knocks, so there is little to maintain across the years a cabin spends standing on site.

The interior is lined with sandwich panel, which does the quieter work. It insulates against both heat and sound, keeping the inside cool in summer and warm in winter, and it damps the noise of a busy entrance or a service yard. That matters when somebody is sitting in the cabin for a full shift.
Glazing that keeps the approach in view

The cabins are generously glazed. Staff can watch the entrance and the traffic in front of them without the shut-in feeling of a small closed structure, and the light coming in makes the interior a more comfortable place to spend a working day.
Delivered ready to connect

There is no assembly. A forklift or crane sets the cabin down where it is wanted, and no groundwork or additional infrastructure is needed to receive it. The electrics, lighting and sockets are fitted at the factory, so the cabin goes into service shortly after it arrives rather than waiting on trades.
The same is true in reverse. When a project finishes, the cabin can be lifted out and moved to the next one, which makes it as workable for a temporary posting as for a permanent gatehouse.
Five sizes, from a single pitch to a small office

The range runs from 1.40m × 1.40m up to 2.65m × 2.65m. The smallest size drops into a confined spot where floor area is short, while still giving one person room to work. From the next size up there is space for a desk, a chair and a small cabinet, which puts it closer to a compact office than a booth. The larger models hold more than one member of staff along with control panels, filing or air conditioning.
Across the range the same cabin serves as a security point, an information or consultation desk, a visitor reception, a ticket office or a temporary office, depending on what the site needs.
Where MetroCity cabins are used
Residential development and apartment entrances
, and the gate points of managed estates.
Shopping centres, hotels and business centres
, as security or reception cabins.
Campuses
— schools, universities, hospitals and sports halls.
Logistics depots, factories, industrial estates and ports.
Municipal service points and public buildings.
Exhibitions, events and festival grounds
, as ticket control or an information point.
Car parks
, where staff need shelter and a clear view of the approach.
Buffet and kiosk points
, including temporary catering and bread distribution counters.

children.text: A moulded polyester shell, built to stand outside

The GRP Cabin is a modular cabin moulded from glass reinforced polyester, and the material is what the range is built around. Polyester holds up against sun, rain and wind, which is what gives the cabin its working life outdoors, and its insulating properties keep the interior comfortable in both summer and winter.

The shell is light for its size. That makes a cabin straightforward to transport and to relocate if the site plan changes later — useful on construction sites and event grounds, where a control point rarely stays in one place for the life of the project.
Delivered ready for use
Cabins arrive complete, so putting one into service is a matter of siting the unit rather than building it. The same holds if it needs to move again.

The range runs from 1.50m × 1.50m up to 2.70m × 2.70m. The smaller sizes suit a confined pitch where one person needs shelter and a clear view of the approach. The wider models give enough floor area for more than one member of staff, and enough room to bring in additional equipment or furniture where the role calls for it.

children.text: Sandwich panel walls, insulated against heat and noise

The Insulated Panel Cabin is built from sandwich panel, and that construction is what the range is organised around. The panel walls hold back heat and sound together, so the person on duty is kept off the worst of the summer and out of the winter cold, and works in a space that is isolated from the noise going on outside it. Wind, rain and direct sun are kept out the same way, which is what lets the cabin stand outdoors for years rather than for a season.

The outside asks very little in return. The cladding wipes clean and needs no routine attention to stay presentable, so a cabin that has been on the gate for a long time still looks like part of the organisation rather than something left over from the last project.
Delivered wired, ready to be sited

Cabins arrive with the electrics already in place — lighting and socket outlets fitted inside, and the connections prepared for mains power and water. Ventilation comes as part of the build. Nothing has to be constructed on site: no foundations, no fitting-out, no second trade after the delivery lorry has gone, which is what makes the range worth considering for short-term work as well as for a permanent post.
Moving one later is equally undemanding. A forklift or a crane lifts the cabin and sets it down wherever it is wanted, and it can be lifted again and reused somewhere else when the site plan changes.
Five sizes, from a single post to a shared office

The range runs from 1.10m × 1.10m up to 2.60m × 2.60m. The smallest models are made for a confined pitch where one person needs shelter and a clear line of sight to the approach, and they take up little enough ground to drop into a gateway or a kerbside that has no room to spare.

The middle of the range gives a single member of staff a proper working position — enough floor for a desk and chair, and for a control panel or the equipment the role happens to need. The largest sizes go further again, holding desks, seating, a cabinet and control screens, and taking several people on duty at once. Generous glazing brings daylight into the larger models, which matters on a long shift.

children.text: An aluminium composite skin over an insulated shell

The KompoCity Composite Cabin is built in two layers: a sandwich panel structure inside, clad on the outside in aluminium composite panel. That cladding is what separates the range from an ordinary site cabin. It stands up to rain, sun and wind, and it avoids the fading and rusting that show up on an exterior surface after a few seasons outdoors.

The inner sandwich panel does the other half of the work. It insulates against heat and sound, so staff on a long shift are not sitting in whatever the weather is doing outside, and the interior lining is chosen to keep even the smaller cabins feeling open rather than boxed in.
A frontage that suits the building behind it

A cabin at the entrance to a development, a hotel or a business centre becomes part of the frontage whether or not anyone intended it to. The composite exterior gives straight lines and a smooth, even surface, which sits closer to the architecture around it than a traditional security booth does. Colour and cladding details can be matched to an organisation's identity, and logos can be applied to the panels.
Modular, so it can move

Cabins are modular and go up quickly once on site. A unit can be lifted with a forklift or crane, taken to another part of the site or to another site entirely, and put back into service there — useful where a control point moves with the phase of a project rather than staying at one gate for good.

Interiors can be prepared before delivery: electrical installation, lighting, sockets and ventilation, with air conditioning infrastructure where the role calls for it. The cabin arrives set up for the job it is going to do.
Five sizes, from a single pitch to a working office

The range runs from 1.40m × 1.40m up to 2.65m × 2.65m. The smallest is sized for one person on duty, and its compact footprint is an advantage in a city centre, a plaza or a shopping centre entrance where there is little floor area to give up. The middle of the range takes a desk, a chair and a document rack. The larger cabins hold a desk, seating, filing, monitors and communications equipment with room to receive a visitor, and there is space for a small sink or an air conditioning unit where the cabin is doing more than watching a gate.

, at car park and restaurant entrances.

— cafeteria counters, ticket and travel card sales, and small service points in areas with heavy foot traffic.

children.text: Betopan outside, sandwich panel inside

The MetroCity Modular Cabin is built from two materials working to different ends. The exterior is clad in Betopan, and that cladding is what the cabin shows to the street. It holds its appearance outdoors — sunlight, rain, humidity and wind leave it without fading, cracking or peeling — and it takes knocks, so there is little to maintain across the years a cabin spends standing on site.

The interior is lined with sandwich panel, which does the quieter work. It insulates against both heat and sound, keeping the inside cool in summer and warm in winter, and it damps the noise of a busy entrance or a service yard. That matters when somebody is sitting in the cabin for a full shift.
Glazing that keeps the approach in view

The cabins are generously glazed. Staff can watch the entrance and the traffic in front of them without the shut-in feeling of a small closed structure, and the light coming in makes the interior a more comfortable place to spend a working day.
Delivered ready to connect

There is no assembly. A forklift or crane sets the cabin down where it is wanted, and no groundwork or additional infrastructure is needed to receive it. The electrics, lighting and sockets are fitted at the factory, so the cabin goes into service shortly after it arrives rather than waiting on trades.
The same is true in reverse. When a project finishes, the cabin can be lifted out and moved to the next one, which makes it as workable for a temporary posting as for a permanent gatehouse.
Five sizes, from a single pitch to a small office

The range runs from 1.40m × 1.40m up to 2.65m × 2.65m. The smallest size drops into a confined spot where floor area is short, while still giving one person room to work. From the next size up there is space for a desk, a chair and a small cabinet, which puts it closer to a compact office than a booth. The larger models hold more than one member of staff along with control panels, filing or air conditioning.
Across the range the same cabin serves as a security point, an information or consultation desk, a visitor reception, a ticket office or a temporary office, depending on what the site needs.
